tool.name: Microsoft Azure
tool.tagline: Microsoft's cloud: compute, data, identity and networking services
tool.description: Microsoft Azure is a public cloud platform offering hundreds of services, from virtual machines and Kubernetes to managed databases, serverless functions, messaging and identity with Microsoft Entra ID. Companies use it to host applications, data platforms and enterprise workloads, especially where Microsoft 365, .NET and Windows Server are already in use. Learning Azure means learning its resource model, identity and RBAC, networking and the managed services that replace undifferentiated infrastructure work.

glossary.def: Your organisation's own space in Microsoft Entra ID, holding its users, groups and apps. Every Azure subscription belongs to exactly one tenant.
One system serving many separate customers at once while keeping each one's data apart.
An optional folder of Azure subscriptions (and of other management groups), used to give access and set rules for many subscriptions at once.
Azure's unit of billing: each subscription gets its own bill and its own limits, and holds resource groups. It belongs to one tenant.
A folder in Azure for resources that are created and deleted together. Every resource is in exactly one; deleting the group deletes everything in it.
In Azure: access, rules or budgets attached at one level (management group, subscription, resource group) automatically apply to everything below it.
In Azure: the level something applies to, such as a management group, subscription, resource group or single resource. It covers everything below it.
In Azure sign-in, short for access token: a temporary digital pass a program sends with each request to prove who it is and what it may use.
A geographic area, such as West Europe, where Microsoft has one or more datacenters. You choose a region for each Azure resource.
One of several separate groups of datacenters inside an Azure region, each with its own power, cooling and network, so one can fail without the others.
Kept running in several availability zones at once by Azure, so the loss of one zone doesn't take the service or its data down.
A second Azure region in the same part of the world linked to a first one (West Europe with North Europe), used for backup copies and staggered updates.
Azure's command-line tool. Its command is az, as in az vm list; it can do everything the Azure portal can.
Azure's website (portal.azure.com) for creating, viewing and managing resources by clicking.
A small language for picking parts out of JSON, used by the Azure CLI's --query option: [].name means the name of every item.
A terminal that opens inside the Azure portal, with the Azure CLI installed and already signed in.
The single Azure API that every tool talks to for creating, changing and deleting resources. It checks who you are and what you may do first.
The Azure service that handles one family of resources, named like Microsoft.Storage or Microsoft.Web. It must be registered in a subscription before use.
A resource's full path in Azure, like /subscriptions/.../resourceGroups/.../providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/name. It names one exact resource.
A setting on an Azure resource, group or subscription that blocks deleting it (CanNotDelete) or any change (ReadOnly), even for Owners.
Microsoft's sign-in service, formerly Azure Active Directory. It keeps the accounts of people and programs and checks who they are for Azure and Microsoft 365.
The description of a program that signs in through Entra ID: its client ID (like a username), its secrets or certificates, and what it may ask for.
A program's account inside an Entra ID tenant: the identity you actually give Azure roles to. Created from an app registration, or by Azure for a managed identity.
An identity for code running in Azure whose secret Azure creates, stores and replaces itself, so nobody ever has to handle a password.
A role such as Global Administrator that controls Entra ID itself (users, groups, apps), as opposed to the Azure roles that control resources.
In Azure: a grant made of three parts: who gets access (security principal), what they may do (role) and where (scope).
Anything Azure can give access to: a user, a group, a service principal or a managed identity.
A named list of allowed actions in Azure, such as Reader or Storage Blob Data Reader, that you give out through role assignments.
The part of a cloud service for managing it: creating, configuring and deleting resources. In Azure these requests go through Azure Resource Manager.
The part of a cloud service for using what's inside it, such as reading files from storage or secrets from a vault. It needs its own permissions.
Infrastructure as a service: renting raw computers, disks and networks from a cloud, while you install and look after the operating system and software.
Platform as a service: you bring your code or data and the cloud runs everything underneath, including servers, updates and scaling.
A virtual processor core given to a VM. A VM size like Standard_D4s_v5 has 4 vCPUs.
An Azure service that lets you log in to your VMs through the portal or CLI without exposing them to the internet.
A VM running on Azure's spare capacity at a large discount, which Azure can take back at short notice. Good for work that can be interrupted.
A setup file a Linux VM runs automatically the first time it starts, used to install and configure software without logging in.
An Azure virtual network: your own private network in one region, with a private IP address range split into subnets.
A short way to write a range of IP addresses, like 10.10.0.0/16: the number after the slash says how many leading bits are fixed, so bigger numbers mean smaller ranges.
A smaller slice of a network's address range, such as 10.10.1.0/24, used to group resources and attach rules to them.
A direct private link between two Azure VNets. It doesn't pass traffic on: if A peers with B and B with C, A can't reach C.
A network security group: a list of allow and deny rules for traffic, attached to a subnet or a VM's network card. The lowest-numbered matching rule wins.
A name such as Internet or Storage.WestEurope that stands for a group of IP addresses Azure keeps up to date, used in network rules instead of raw numbers.
An Azure resource that lets VMs in a subnet reach the internet through one fixed public IP address, without being reachable from it.
An Azure resource with a globally unique name that holds blobs, queues, file shares and tables, with a chosen performance and number of copies.
Azure's word for a product variant and its price tier, such as Standard_ZRS for storage or Standard_D4s_v5 for a VM.
Locally redundant storage: Azure keeps three copies of your data in one datacenter.
Zone-redundant storage: three copies of your data, one in each of three availability zones of the region, written at the same time.
Geo-redundant storage: three copies in one datacenter plus a copy in the paired region, updated a moment later. RA-GRS also lets you read that far copy.
Geo-zone-redundant storage: copies across three availability zones plus a copy in the paired region, updated a moment later.
One of a storage account's two master passwords. Whoever holds one has full control of the account, so it's safer to turn them off and use Entra ID.
Azure's name for a file stored in Blob Storage, of any type or size, kept under a name inside a blob container.
A named bucket of blobs inside a storage account, like a top-level folder. Nothing to do with Docker containers.
A storage account option that gives Blob Storage real folders that can be renamed in one step, as data-analysis tools need. Sold as Data Lake Storage.
How a blob is priced: Hot, Cool, Cold or Archive. Colder tiers are cheaper to store but cost more, and take longer, to read.
Copying a blob from the offline Archive tier back to an online tier so it can be read; it can take hours.
Rules on a storage account that move blobs to colder tiers or delete them automatically as they get older.
Shared access signature: a URL with permissions and an expiry time built in and signed, so whoever holds it can use one storage item without your login.
A SAS signed with a key obtained through an Entra ID login rather than the account key, so it can be traced and cancelled on its own.
Keeping deleted items for a set number of days so they can be restored, instead of destroying them at once.
Azure's service for running websites and web APIs from your code or container image, without managing the servers underneath.
The computing power behind App Service apps: operating system, pricing tier and number of instances. You pay for the plan; several apps can share it.
Named settings stored with an Azure web app or function app, which the code reads as environment variables.
An extra live copy of an App Service app (such as staging) with its own address, which can be swapped with production in one step.
An App Service setting that keeps the app loaded even when nobody is using it, so the next visitor doesn't wait for it to start.
One billable measurement in Azure, such as VM hours, gigabytes stored per month or data sent out. Your bill is the sum of all meters.
In Azure: a spending amount for a subscription or resource group that sends alerts at chosen levels. It never stops resources by itself.
A saved Azure list of whom to notify (email, text message) and what to run when an alert or budget fires.
An Azure service that reviews your resources and suggests savings and fixes, such as resizing idle VMs.
Data leaving a network or cloud, for example sent from Azure to users on the internet. Clouds usually charge for it per gigabyte.
A special address (169.254.169.254) reachable only from inside an Azure VM, where code can ask about the VM and get access tokens for its managed identity.
A class in Azure's SDKs that tries several sign-in methods in turn (environment variables, managed identity, your Azure CLI login...), so the same code works locally and in Azure.
Azure's guarded store for secrets, encryption keys and certificates, read through Azure roles and managed identities.
Hardware security module: tamper-proof hardware that stores encryption keys and uses them internally, so the keys can never be copied out.
A Key Vault setting that stops anyone from permanently deleting soft-deleted vaults, keys or secrets before the retention period ends.
An app setting written as @Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=...): the platform fetches the secret with the app's identity and gives it to the code as an environment variable.
Azure's own language for describing resources in text files. A Bicep file is converted to an ARM template and deployed by Azure Resource Manager.
In Azure: a file describing resources to deploy, either a JSON ARM template or a Bicep file that is converted into one.
The short name a Bicep file gives a resource (like sa) so other parts of the file can refer to it, as in sa.id.
Ready-made, tested Bicep and Terraform modules published by Microsoft for common Azure resources.
A preview of an Azure deployment that lists what would be created, changed or deleted, without changing anything.
In Azure Functions: the one event that starts a function, such as an HTTP request, a timer or a new queue message.
In Azure Functions: a declared link to another service that reads data in or writes data out for the function, without hand-written connection code.
The Azure resource that holds a group of functions which are deployed, configured and scaled together.
Azure Functions' serverless hosting plans: you pay per run and instances are added or removed automatically, down to zero. Flex is the newer, recommended one.
An extension of Azure Functions for long, multi-step workflows: it saves progress between steps so the workflow can wait and resume.
Azure's service for running containers without managing servers or Kubernetes, with built-in HTTPS access, revisions and automatic scaling.
Popular open-source software that runs and manages many containers across a group of machines, restarting, spreading and scaling them.
The way requests get into an app from outside: which address and port accept traffic and where it goes. Opposite of egress.
In Container Apps: a frozen version of an app's settings and image. Each change creates a new revision, and traffic can be split between them.
Releasing a new version to a small share of users first (say 10%) and only sending everyone once it proves healthy.
Kubernetes event-driven autoscaling: open-source software that adds or removes container copies based on signals like queue length, including down to zero.
Azure Container Registry: Azure's private registry for container images. The AcrPull role lets an identity download images from it.
Microsoft's SQL Server database engine run by Azure, with updates, backups and standby copies handled for you.
In Azure SQL: the address you connect to (name.database.windows.net) and a home for shared settings, holding one or more databases.
A virtual processor core used to size and price databases such as Azure SQL; you choose how many.
In Azure SQL: a copy of databases kept in another region, with one connection name that always points at whichever copy is currently in charge.
Azure's NoSQL database for JSON documents, which can keep copies in many regions and answers in milliseconds at any size.
In Cosmos DB: all items sharing one partition key value, such as one customer's orders. At most 20 GB.
In Cosmos DB: one of the machines-worth of storage and capacity that logical partitions are spread over. Each serves up to 10,000 RU/s and 50 GB.
In Cosmos DB: fetching one item by its id and partition key value, the cheapest and fastest operation.
Cosmos DB's unit of work: reading one 1 KB item by id costs 1 RU. You reserve or pay for RUs per second.
The simple message queue built into an Azure storage account, for large numbers of small messages.
How long a queue message stays hidden after a program takes it. If it isn't deleted by then, it reappears so it can be tried again.
Azure's managed shared network drives (file shares) that computers and containers can attach over SMB or NFS.
The standard protocol Windows (and also macOS and Linux) uses to open files on shared network drives.
Network File System: the standard way Linux and Unix computers attach shared network drives.
A service that keeps copies of an Azure file share on your own Windows servers for fast local access.
Azure's message broker for important business messages, with queues, topics, ordered sessions, dead-lettering and transactions.
A named channel in a message broker: senders publish to it once and every subscription to it receives its own copy.
Service Bus's default way of receiving: the message is locked for one receiver, which must then complete, abandon or dead-letter it.
A side queue where messages that can't be delivered or processed are parked, so they stop blocking others and someone can inspect them.
Azure's umbrella service for measurements, logs and alerts about your resources and applications.
Azure's store for log records, searched with the KQL query language. Resources send logs there through diagnostic settings.
Kusto Query Language: the query language for Azure logs. A query starts from a table and passes rows through steps joined by the | character.
A setting on an Azure resource that sends its logs and measurements somewhere, usually a Log Analytics workspace. Without one, the logs aren't kept.
The part of Azure Monitor that watches an application: its requests, outgoing calls, errors, log lines and response times.
An open standard and set of libraries for collecting traces, measurements and logs from applications, supported by Azure Monitor and many other tools.
An Azure resource that manages a group of VMs created from one configuration, adding or removing them automatically.
A regular check a load balancer or Front Door sends to each server; only servers that answer correctly receive traffic.
A filter in front of a web app that inspects HTTP requests and blocks common attacks, such as attempts to slip database commands into forms.
Azure's regional load balancer for HTTP: it reads requests, can route by path, handles HTTPS and can include a web application firewall.
A private IP address inside your VNet that leads to one specific Azure service, so traffic to it never crosses the public internet. Built on Azure Private Link.
A virtual network card: the Azure resource that gives a VM or private endpoint its IP address inside a subnet.
A DNS record saying one name is an alias of another: look up the other name instead.
A set of DNS records that only the Azure VNets linked to it can see, used to give private endpoints their names.
The basic DNS record that maps a hostname to an IP address.
An older Azure option that lets a service recognise and allow traffic from one of your subnets, while the service keeps its public IP address.
Azure's service for delivering small event notifications (a blob was created, a resource changed) to the code that wants to react, by calling it.
In Event Grid: a source of events. System topics are events Azure services publish about themselves; custom topics are ones your own apps publish.
In Event Grid: a rule saying which events from a topic to deliver, and to which receiver.
An open standard format for event messages, so events from different systems look alike. Recommended for Event Grid.
Azure's service for very high-volume streams of events, kept for days so readers can process them at their own pace and re-read history. Accepts Kafka clients.
Azure Kubernetes Service: a Kubernetes cluster where Azure runs the control plane and you manage the node pools and workloads.
Kubernetes' smallest unit: one or a few containers that are started, scheduled and stopped together on one node.
In Kubernetes: one worker machine (in AKS, a VM) that runs pods.
The command-line tool for talking to a Kubernetes cluster: listing, creating and inspecting pods, nodes and other objects.
Service level agreement: a provider's written promise of how reliable a service will be (for example 99.95% uptime), with money back if it's missed.
In AKS: a group of nodes of one VM size, built on a scale set. The system pool runs the cluster's own add-ons; user pools run your workloads.
An AKS networking mode where pods get IP addresses from a separate private range rather than from your VNet, so a big cluster doesn't use up VNet addresses.
Azure's API gateway service: a single entrance in front of your APIs that checks callers, limits rates, changes requests and documents the APIs.
A single entrance that all requests to a set of services pass through, where shared checks such as sign-in and rate limits happen.
In API Management: a key a consumer gets when subscribing to a product and sends with each call to identify themselves.
Azure's worldwide entrance for web traffic: it answers close to users, caches content, filters attacks and forwards to your servers in whichever region is healthy.
One of many small sites around the world, close to users, where a provider answers requests and caches content.
Announcing one IP address from many places at once, so each user's traffic automatically goes to the nearest one.
In Front Door or a CDN: the real server that runs your app and answers the requests the edge forwards.
An Azure service that steers users between regions with DNS alone, handing out the address of a healthy region without touching the traffic itself.
Azure's service for rules about resource settings: it can block, change or report resources that break them.
One Azure Policy rule: an if condition on resource settings plus an effect such as Deny, Audit, Modify or DeployIfNotExists.
A named set of Azure Policy definitions assigned together, such as a security standard.
A recorded waiver that excuses one resource or scope from an Azure Policy assignment, ideally with an end date.
A run of an Azure Policy's fix (Modify or DeployIfNotExists) on resources that already existed when the policy was assigned.
The HTTP method meaning create this thing, or replace it entirely with what I'm sending. Azure Resource Manager uses it for every resource it deploys.
ARM's default deployment mode: resources in the resource group that aren't in the template are left alone.
An ARM deployment mode that deletes every resource in the resource group that isn't in the template.
An Azure feature that manages a deployed set of resources as one unit, cleaning up resources removed from the template and blocking changes made outside it.
A subscription prepared in advance with networking, identity, policy and monitoring, so an application team can deploy into it safely from day one.
Automatically creating and wiring up a new subscription (management group, network, budgets, roles) from code when a team requests one.
Letting code outside Azure (a deployment pipeline, a Kubernetes pod, another cloud) get Entra tokens by trading in a signed token from its own platform, with no stored secret.
A setting on a managed identity or app registration naming an outside token issuer and subject that Entra ID will trust in place of a secret.
In Cosmos DB: a partition that gets far more traffic than the others, so it hits its limit while the rest of the container sits idle.
In Cosmos DB: how up to date a read is guaranteed to be, from Strong (always the latest) down to Eventual (all copies agree in the end).
A Cosmos DB mode where every region accepts writes, so apps are fast everywhere but conflicting changes must be settled.
In Cosmos DB: an ordered list of every change to a container's items, which code can read to react to changes or keep other data in step.
A 1- or 3-year commitment to a specific Azure resource type and region in exchange for a large discount.
A commitment to spend a fixed amount per hour on Azure compute (or databases) for 1 or 3 years, applied across sizes, regions and services for a discount.
A discount for reusing Windows Server or SQL Server licences you already own on Azure resources.
A cost view that spreads an up-front commitment's price evenly over the hours and resources that used it, instead of showing it all on the purchase day.
Running cloud cost as an ongoing shared practice between engineering and finance: owners, budgets, regular reviews and alerts.
Recovery time objective: how long a system may stay down after a failure before it must be working again.
Recovery point objective: how much recent data (measured in time) you may lose in a failure.
A multi-region design where one region serves all traffic and a second waits ready (on standby) to take over if the first fails.
A multi-region design where two or more regions serve traffic at the same time, so losing one only removes part of the capacity.
An Azure service that deliberately injects failures (a zone outage, a slow network) into your system so you can test how it copes.

concepts.name: Tenants, subscriptions and resource groups
concepts.summary: How Azure organizes everything: a tenant, management groups, subscriptions, resource groups and resources.
concepts.why: Every permission, rule and budget in Azure is attached to one level of this hierarchy and applies to everything below it.
concepts.body:
In Azure you rent computing pieces from Microsoft: a virtual machine, a database, space to store files. Each such piece is called a resource. A real company soon has thousands of them, so Azure files them in a strict hierarchy, like folders inside folders, and almost every other feature hangs off it.

From the top down:

- **Tenant**: your organisation's own space in Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft's sign-in service. It holds your people and their logins. Most organisations have exactly one.
- **Management groups**: optional folders of subscriptions, nested up to six levels deep, used to set access and rules for many subscriptions at once.
- **Subscription**: the unit of billing. Each subscription gets its own bill and its own **quotas**: limits on how much you may create, such as how many processor cores you can run in one place. A subscription belongs to exactly one tenant.
- **Resource group**: a folder for resources that are created and deleted together. Every resource lives in exactly one resource group, and deleting the group deletes everything inside it.
- **Resource**: a VM, a file store, a database and so on.

Access, rules and budgets that you attach to one level are **inherited**: they automatically apply to everything below it. Give someone read access on a subscription and they can read every resource group and resource in it. Later lessons cover permissions and rules in detail.

A resource group is created in a region (a place where Microsoft has datacenters, see the next lesson), but that only decides where Azure keeps the group's own bookkeeping. The resources inside can live in any region.

Group resources by what is created and deleted together, not by kind: one group "orders-api-prod" holding an app, its database and its storage beats one group "all-databases". Teams also usually keep production and everything else in separate subscriptions, so their bills, limits and access stay apart.
concepts.code:
# List the subscriptions you can see, as a table
az account list --query "[].{name:name, id:id, tenant:tenantId}" -o table
az account set --subscription "Contoso Dev"   # work in this one from now on

az group create --name rg-orders-dev --location westeurope
az group list --query "[].name" -o tsv
# rg-orders-dev

# Deleting the group deletes every resource inside it
az group delete --name rg-orders-dev --yes --no-wait
takeaways: Tenant > management groups > subscriptions > resource groups > resources
Access, rules and budgets are inherited by everything below
A subscription is the unit of billing and of quotas
Group resources by shared lifecycle, not by type
pitfalls: Putting unrelated workloads in one resource group, so you cannot delete one, or give access to one, without the other.

quiz.q: A user is given permission to change resources on a subscription. What can they change?
options: Every resource group and resource in that subscription
Nothing until each resource group grants access
quiz.explain: Access given at one level is inherited by every level below it.

quiz.q: What happens to a storage account in westeurope inside a resource group whose location is eastus?
options: Nothing unusual: the group's location only says where its bookkeeping is kept
The account is moved to eastus
It is billed at eastus prices
quiz.explain: Resources in a group may live in any region; the group's own location is only for its bookkeeping.

concepts.name: Regions, availability zones and pairs
concepts.summary: Where Azure resources physically run, and how availability zones and paired regions protect you from failures.
concepts.why: Picking regions and zones decides how fast your app feels to users, which failures it survives, where its data legally lives, and even the price.
concepts.body:
Azure is made of real buildings full of computers, called datacenters, spread around the world. A **region** is a group of datacenters in one area, such as `westeurope` (the Netherlands) or `eastus2` (Virginia). You pick a region for each resource, and the choice matters: users far away wait longer for every answer, some countries require data to stay inside their borders, and services and prices differ between regions.

Many regions are split into **availability zones**: three or more separate groups of datacenters a few kilometres apart, each with its own power, cooling and network, joined by very fast links. A fire or power cut in one zone leaves the others running. Resources use zones in two ways:

- **Zonal**: pinned to one zone you pick (`--zone 1`), such as a VM. To survive a zone failure you run copies in several zones yourself.
- **Zone-redundant**: Azure keeps copies in several zones for you, as with zone-redundant storage or databases.

Zone numbers are per subscription: your zone 1 may be a different building from someone else's zone 1.

Many regions also have a **paired region** in the same part of the world (West Europe with North Europe). Some services can keep a second copy of your data in the pair, and Microsoft updates only one region of a pair at a time, so one bad update can't hit both. Newer regions may have no pair; you can still choose any second region you like.

Keeping copies of data in several places is called **replication**. Zones are close together, so copies there can be updated at the same instant and a zone failure loses nothing. A second region is far away, so its copy is updated a moment later and trails slightly behind; if the first region is lost, the last few seconds of changes may be lost too.

Switching users over to the backup copy when the main one fails is called **failover**. Rule of thumb: zones protect you against one datacenter failing, almost for free; a second region protects against a whole region going down, but needs a planned and practised failover.
concepts.code:
# Which regions does my subscription see, and which have zones?
az account list-locations \
  --query "[?metadata.regionType=='Physical'].{name:name, pair:metadata.pairedRegion[0].name}" -o table

# A VM pinned to zone 2
az vm create -g rg-demo -n vm-z2 --image Ubuntu2404 --zone 2 \
  --admin-username azureuser --generate-ssh-keys
takeaways: Region = where it runs; zone = which independent datacenter group inside that region
Zonal resources are pinned to one zone; zone-redundant ones are copied across zones for you
Zones guard against a datacenter failure, a second region against a whole-region outage
pitfalls: Deploying three VMs "so one can fail" all in the same zone, or with no zone at all.

quiz.q: You need to survive the loss of a single datacenter with no data loss and little slowdown. What do you use?
options: A paired region whose copy trails slightly behind
quiz.explain: Zones are separate datacenters in one region, close enough that copies can be kept exactly in step.

concepts.name: How programs talk: IP addresses, URLs and APIs
concepts.summary: The networking words every Azure lesson uses: IP addresses, DNS, HTTP requests and status codes, HTTPS, URLs and APIs.
concepts.why: Everything in Azure is reached over a network, so these few ideas come up in every service you'll use.
concepts.body:
Almost everything in Azure is used over a network: your laptop sends a message to a computer in a Microsoft datacenter, and that computer answers. From Docker you know a server is a program waiting for clients on a numbered port. This lesson fills in how computers find each other and what their messages look like.

Every computer on a network has an **IP address**, a number such as `20.13.45.7` that works like a street address for data. Addresses starting with `10.` or `192.168.` are private: they only work inside one organisation's network, like room numbers inside a building. Most others are public, reachable from anywhere on the internet.

Numbers are hard to remember, so computers also get names. `example.com` is a **domain name**; the full name of one machine or service, like `mystore.blob.core.windows.net`, is a **hostname**.

**DNS** is the internet's phone book: a program asks it for a hostname and gets back that name's IP address. Every connection starts with this lookup.

Programs on the web talk using **HTTP**. The client sends a **request** ("give me this", "save this") and the server sends back a **response**.

Every response starts with a three-digit **status code** saying how it went: 200 means OK, 401 "I don't know who you are", 403 "I know who you are, but you're not allowed", 404 "not found", 429 "too many requests, slow down".

**HTTPS** is HTTP with **encryption**: the data is scrambled on the way so nobody in between can read or change it. The scrambling standard is called **TLS**; Azure services require TLS version 1.2 or newer.

To prove it really is, say, Microsoft's server and not an impostor, the server shows a **certificate**: a digital ID card for its hostname, signed by a trusted authority. Your **browser** (Chrome, Edge, Safari) checks it before showing the padlock icon.

A **URL** is the full address of one thing on the web. `https://mystore.blob.core.windows.net/photos/cat.jpg` says: use HTTPS, find that hostname, ask for `/photos/cat.jpg`.

An **API** is the set of requests a service agrees to answer, a menu for programs instead of people. Each URL on that menu that does one job is an **endpoint**. Azure itself is controlled through such an API: the website, the `az` command and every other tool send HTTPS requests to it.
concepts.code:
# Ask DNS for the IP address behind a hostname
nslookup learn.microsoft.com
# Name:    ...
# Address: 23.x.x.x

# Send an HTTPS request to Azure's API without signing in,
# and print only the status code of the response
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" \
  "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions?api-version=2022-12-01"
# 401   <- the API answered: "I don't know who you are"
takeaways: IP address = where a machine is; DNS turns names into IP addresses
HTTP: a client sends a request, the server returns a response with a status code
HTTPS = HTTP plus TLS encryption, with a certificate proving the server's identity
An API is the menu of requests a service answers; each URL on it is an endpoint
pitfalls: Mixing up 401 and 403: 401 means you didn't prove who you are, 403 means you did but lack permission.

quiz.q: Your program gets status code 403 from an Azure service. What does it mean?
options: The service knows who you are, but you don't have permission
quiz.explain: 403 means forbidden: you are identified but not allowed; 401 would mean not identified.

quiz.q: What does DNS do?
options: Turns a hostname into an IP address
quiz.explain: DNS is the phone book that maps names to the numeric addresses computers use.

concepts.name: Azure CLI essentials
concepts.summary: Sign in, pick a subscription, create resources and shape the output with --query and -o.
concepts.why: The CLI is the fastest way to explore Azure, and commands you try by hand can later be saved and rerun automatically.
concepts.body:
The **Azure CLI** is a command-line tool, like `docker`, whose command is `az`. It runs on Windows, macOS and Linux and can do everything the Azure website, the **Azure portal**, can. Behind the scenes, each `az` command sends HTTPS requests to Azure's API.

Commands read `az <area> <sub-area> <action>`: `az storage account create`, `az vm list`, `az webapp log tail`. Add `--help` to any command to see its options and examples.

Getting started:

- `az login` opens your browser so you can sign in (on a machine without a browser, add `--use-device-code` and type the code it shows on another device).
- `az account show` prints the subscription you're working in; `az account set -s <name or id>` switches to another.
- `az configure --defaults group=rg-demo location=westeurope` remembers a resource group and region, so you don't type `-g` and `-l` every time.

Output is JSON by default. `-o table` prints a readable table and `-o tsv` prints bare values, one per line. `--query` picks out and reshapes parts of the JSON with a small language called **JMESPath**: `[].name` means "the name of every item in the list". The picking happens on your computer, after the answer arrives.

A common trick is to save one value in a shell **variable**, a named slot that holds a value: `ID=$(az ... -o tsv)`, and later commands use `$ID`. Commands saved in a file and run together form a **script**, the usual way to automate Azure.

**Cloud Shell**, a terminal inside the portal, has `az` installed and already signed in, which is handy on someone else's computer.

When a program rather than a person runs `az`, for example an automatic nightly deployment, never sign it in with your personal account. Later lessons show how to give the program an identity of its own.
concepts.code:
az login
az account set --subscription "Contoso Dev"
az configure --defaults group=rg-demo location=westeurope

az group create --name rg-demo
az storage account create --name stdemo$RANDOM --sku Standard_LRS

# JMESPath: name and SKU of every storage account, as a table
az storage account list --query "[].{name:name, sku:sku.name}" -o table

# Save one value in a variable
ID=$(az storage account list --query "[0].id" -o tsv)
echo "$ID"   # /subscriptions/.../resourceGroups/rg-demo/providers/Microsoft.Storage/...
takeaways: Commands read az <area> <action>; add --help to anything
--query (JMESPath) picks out parts of the output; -o tsv prints bare values for variables
az configure --defaults removes repetitive -g/-l flags
pitfalls: Picking values out of the JSON output with text-search tools such as grep instead of using --query.

quiz.q: Which command prints only the names of all resource groups, one per line?
quiz.explain: --query selects the name field from every element and -o tsv prints plain lines.

concepts.name: Resource Manager, IDs, tags and locks
concepts.summary: Azure Resource Manager is the one API behind the portal, the CLI and every other tool; learn resource IDs, providers, tags and locks.
concepts.why: Understanding ARM explains why every tool behaves the same, and how to label resources and protect them from accidents.
concepts.body:
Whether you click in the portal, type an `az` command or run a program, every request to create, change or delete something goes to the same place: **Azure Resource Manager (ARM)**, Azure's single API at `https://management.azure.com`. That's why all the tools behave alike.

ARM handles each request in steps. First it checks who you are; this is **authentication**, done through Entra ID. Then it checks that you're allowed to do this, using your permissions and your organisation's rules.

Only then does it pass the request to a **resource provider**: the Azure service that owns that kind of resource, such as `Microsoft.Storage` for storage or `Microsoft.Web` for web apps.

Every resource has a **resource ID**, its complete address in the hierarchy:

`/subscriptions/{sub}/resourceGroups/{rg}/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/{name}`

You pass that ID (with `--ids` or `--scope`) whenever a command must point at one exact resource. A provider has to be switched on, or registered, in a subscription before use. Most are registered automatically; the error "MissingSubscriptionRegistration" means you run `az provider register`.

**Tags** are labels made of a name and a value (`env=prod`, `costCenter=1234`). They let you split the bill by team and find resources from scripts. Unlike access, tags on a resource group are not inherited by the resources inside it.

**Locks** guard against accidents. A `CanNotDelete` lock allows changes but blocks deletion; a `ReadOnly` lock blocks every change. Locks apply to everyone, even Owners (the most powerful role), and are inherited downward.

Be careful with `ReadOnly`: a few actions that only fetch information, such as listing a storage account's keys, are sent to ARM as if they were changes, so the lock blocks them too.
concepts.code:
# Is the Container Apps provider switched on in this subscription?
az provider show -n Microsoft.App --query registrationState -o tsv   # NotRegistered
az provider register -n Microsoft.App

# Add two tags, keeping any existing ones
az resource tag --is-incremental --tags env=prod costCenter=1234 \
  --ids /subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/rg-prod/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/stprod01

# Find everything tagged env=prod
az resource list --tag env=prod --query "[].name" -o tsv

# Nobody, not even an Owner, can delete the group until the lock is removed
az lock create --name no-delete --lock-type CanNotDelete --resource-group rg-prod
takeaways: The portal, the CLI and all other tools send their requests to the same ARM API
Resource IDs encode subscription, group, provider, type and name
Tags label resources for cost reports and automation; they are not inherited by default
CanNotDelete and ReadOnly locks apply even to Owners
pitfalls: Using `az resource tag` without `--is-incremental`, which replaces all existing tags instead of adding to them.

quiz.q: An Owner tries to delete a resource group with a CanNotDelete lock. What happens?
options: It succeeds because Owners bypass locks
It fails until the lock is removed
It succeeds after a 7-day soft-delete period
quiz.explain: Locks apply to all users; an Owner must remove the lock first.

concepts.name: Microsoft Entra ID: identities
concepts.summary: Users, groups, app registrations and service principals: the identities Azure checks before letting anyone in.
concepts.why: Every sign-in to Azure, by a person or a program, is an Entra ID identity, so you need to know the kinds.
concepts.body:
Before Azure does anything for you, it needs to know who is asking. **Microsoft Entra ID** (formerly Azure Active Directory) is Microsoft's sign-in service: it keeps the list of accounts and checks passwords and other proof of who you are. A service that does this job for other services is called an **identity provider**; Entra ID is the one behind Azure, Microsoft 365 and, if you like, your own apps.

Your organisation's space in Entra ID is its tenant. The kinds of identity you'll meet there start with people:

- **Users**: people, either members of your organisation or invited guests from other organisations.
- **Groups**: named collections of users and other identities. Give access to groups rather than to single people, so a newcomer only has to join the group.

Programs need identities too, such as a tool that deploys your app every night. For that you create an **app registration**: the description of the program, with an ID (its client ID, which works like a username) and a **secret**, a password-like string the program uses to prove who it is.

An app registration is only a description. The account you actually give permissions to is its **service principal**: the program's identity inside your tenant, created along with the app registration (the portal lists them under "Enterprise applications").

A **managed identity** goes one step further: a service principal whose secret Azure creates, stores and replaces by itself, so no person ever handles it. A later lesson covers it.

Keep two permission systems apart. **Entra roles** (Global Administrator, User Administrator) control the directory itself: who can create users or reset passwords. Azure roles (Owner, Contributor, Reader, next lesson) control Azure resources. A Global Administrator has no access to subscriptions by default.

After you sign in, Entra ID hands your tool an **access token**: a digital pass, valid for about an hour, that says who you are and which service it's for, like a wristband at an event. The tool sends it with every request, for example to Azure's management API at `https://management.azure.com/`.
concepts.code:
# Who am I signed in as?
az ad signed-in-user show --query "{upn:userPrincipalName, id:id}"

# A group to give access to
az ad group create --display-name "orders-devs" --mail-nickname orders-devs

# An app registration, then its service principal
APP_ID=$(az ad app create --display-name orders-ci --query appId -o tsv)
az ad sp create --id "$APP_ID"

# Get an access token for ARM as the signed-in user; print when it expires
az account get-access-token --resource https://management.azure.com/ --query expiresOn
takeaways: A tenant is your organisation's one Entra ID directory
App registration = the program's description; service principal = its identity in a tenant
Entra roles govern the directory; Azure roles govern resources
Give access to groups, not to individual users
pitfalls: Assuming a Global Administrator can manage subscriptions: they must first give themselves extra access or be granted an Azure role.

quiz.q: An automatic deployment tool needs permission to create resources. What do you give the Azure role to?
quiz.explain: Roles are given to identities; for a program, that identity is its service principal.

quiz.q: Which statement is true?
options: Entra roles manage the directory, Azure roles manage resources
Global Administrator automatically owns all subscriptions
Azure roles and Entra roles are the same system
quiz.explain: They are separate systems with separate roles and separate places they apply.

concepts.name: Azure RBAC: roles and scopes
concepts.summary: Grant just enough access with role assignments: who (security principal), what (role) and where (scope).
concepts.why: Role-based access control decides who can do what to every resource; getting it right is the core of Azure security.
concepts.body:
Azure controls access with **role-based access control (RBAC)**: instead of listing permissions person by person, you hand out ready-made bundles of permissions called roles. You give a role through a **role assignment**, which has three parts:

- **Security principal** (who): a user, group, service principal or managed identity.
- **Role definition** (what): the list of allowed actions, such as `Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/write`.
- **Scope** (where): a management group, subscription, resource group or single resource.

Assignments only ever add permissions, and they are inherited by everything below their scope. What you can do is everything all your assignments allow, added together. Azure itself can create "deny" rules in a few special cases, but you can't write them directly.

Built-in roles to know: **Owner** (everything, including giving access to others), **Contributor** (everything except giving access), **Reader** (look, don't touch), and many narrow roles for one service, such as **Storage Blob Data Reader** or **Key Vault Secrets User**.

Azure separates managing a resource from using the data inside it. Managing it (creating a storage account, changing its settings) is the **control plane**. Using what's inside (reading the stored files) is the **data plane**, and needs roles of its own.

So Contributor on a storage account lets you reconfigure it, but reading its files with your Entra login still needs a data role such as Storage Blob Data Reader. Role definitions list the two kinds separately, as `Actions` and `DataActions`.

Follow **least privilege**: give each person or program only the access it truly needs. In practice, assign roles to groups, at the narrowest scope that works, and prefer a narrow service role over Contributor. For very powerful roles, Entra's Privileged Identity Management lets people switch a role on for a few hours only when they need it. New assignments can take a few minutes to start working.
concepts.code:
GROUP_ID=$(az ad group show --group orders-devs --query id -o tsv)
RG_ID=$(az group show -n rg-orders-dev --query id -o tsv)

# Contributor on one resource group only
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$GROUP_ID" \
  --assignee-principal-type Group --role Contributor --scope "$RG_ID"

# Data-plane access: read the files in one storage account
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$GROUP_ID" \
  --assignee-principal-type Group --role "Storage Blob Data Reader" \
  --scope "$RG_ID/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/stordersdev"

az role assignment list --scope "$RG_ID" --query "[].{who:principalName, role:roleDefinitionName}" -o table
takeaways: Role assignment = security principal + role + scope
Permissions add up and are inherited by everything below the scope
Managing a resource (control plane) and using its data (data plane) need different roles
Owner can give access to others; Contributor cannot
pitfalls: Giving a program Contributor on a whole subscription when it only needs to read secrets from one Key Vault.

quiz.q: A user has Contributor on a storage account and gets status 403 reading a file in it with their Entra login. Why?
options: Roles do not apply to storage
Contributor covers managing the account (control plane), not reading its data (data plane)
quiz.explain: Reading stored data with an Entra login needs a data role such as Storage Blob Data Reader.

quiz.q: Which built-in role can manage resources but cannot give roles to others?
quiz.explain: Contributor has every action except creating role assignments.

concepts.name: Virtual machines
concepts.summary: Create and manage Linux VMs: images, sizes, disks, logging in with SSH, and what you pay for.
concepts.why: A VM is the most basic way to run anything in Azure, a whole rented computer, and the fallback for whatever doesn't fit a ready-made service.
concepts.body:
You know a virtual machine is a whole pretend computer running on a real one. An Azure VM runs in Microsoft's datacenter. Azure provides the hardware; you choose the operating system and look after it: updates, security fixes and everything you install. Renting raw computers like this is called **infrastructure as a service (IaaS)**.

What you choose:

- **Image**: the operating system to start from, such as Ubuntu 24.04 (`Ubuntu2404` for short) or Windows Server. Same idea as a Docker image, but for a whole computer.
- **Size**: how much processing power and memory. The first letter gives the shape: B (cheap, for light use), D (general purpose), E (extra memory), F (extra processing), N (with a **GPU**, a graphics chip that is also good at heavy number-crunching). `Standard_D4s_v5` has 4 virtual processors, or **vCPUs**.
- **Disks**: one holding the operating system, plus optional data disks. Faster kinds (Premium SSD, Ultra) cost more.
- **Network**: an address in a private Azure network (a later lesson) and, optionally, a public IP address reachable from the internet.

To work on a Linux VM you log in with **SSH**, an encrypted connection that gives you a terminal on the remote machine. `--generate-ssh-keys` creates a matching pair of key files that acts as a password you never type. Leaving SSH open to the whole internet invites attacks, so production setups use **Azure Bastion** (a guarded login gateway reached through the portal) or Entra ID login instead.

You pay per second while the VM holds hardware for you, plus the disks all the time. The trap: shutting down from inside the operating system, or `az vm stop`, keeps the hardware reserved, so you keep paying for it. `az vm deallocate` gives the hardware back and stops the compute charges; the disks still cost money.

Two more tools. **Spot VMs** run on Azure's spare capacity at a deep discount, but Azure can take them back at short notice, so they suit work that can be interrupted and restarted. **cloud-init** (`--custom-data`) runs a setup file the first time a Linux VM starts, so your software gets installed without anyone logging in.
concepts.code:
az vm create -g rg-demo -n vm-web01 \
  --image Ubuntu2404 --size Standard_B2s \
  --admin-username azureuser --generate-ssh-keys \
  --public-ip-sku Standard --custom-data cloud-init.yaml

az vm open-port -g rg-demo -n vm-web01 --port 80   # let web traffic in
az vm list -d -o table --query "[].{name:name, state:powerState, ip:publicIps}"
# vm-web01  VM running  20.13.x.x

az vm stop -g rg-demo -n vm-web01        # hardware still reserved: still billed
az vm deallocate -g rg-demo -n vm-web01  # compute billing stops; disks still billed
takeaways: You manage the operating system and everything above it
Size letters describe the shape (B, D, E, F, N)
Only deallocate stops compute charges
Use Bastion or Entra login rather than SSH open to the internet
pitfalls: Shutting a VM down from inside its operating system and assuming billing has stopped.

quiz.q: Which action stops compute billing for a VM?
options: sudo shutdown -h now inside the VM
quiz.explain: Only deallocating gives the hardware back; stop keeps it reserved for you.

concepts.name: VNets, subnets and NSGs
concepts.summary: Build private networks with address ranges and subnets, and filter traffic with network security groups.
concepts.why: Almost every production workload sits in a VNet, and NSGs are the first layer of network security.
concepts.body:
Resources that talk to each other, like a VM and its database, need a network. In Azure you build your own private one: a **virtual network (VNet)**, which lives in one region. You give it a range of private IP addresses, written like `10.10.0.0/16`.

That way of writing a range is **CIDR**. Inside the computer, an address like 10.10.0.0 is stored as 32 bits (ones and zeros), 8 for each of its four numbers. The number after the slash says how many of those bits, from the left, are the same for every address in the range. `/16` fixes the first two numbers, so `10.10.0.0/16` covers 10.10.0.0 to 10.10.255.255, about 65,000 addresses. `/24` fixes the first three, so `10.10.1.0/24` covers 10.10.1.0 to 10.10.1.255: 256 addresses. A bigger number after the slash means a smaller range.

You split the VNet's range into **subnets**, smaller ranges such as `10.10.1.0/24`, and group resources by subnet: website VMs in one, databases in another. Azure keeps 5 addresses of every subnet for itself, and some services need a whole subnet of their own, so leave plenty of room.

Resources in one VNet can reach each other by default. Two VNets can be joined by **peering**, but peering doesn't pass traffic along: if A is peered with B and B with C, A still can't reach C. Large setups therefore connect every VNet to one central "hub" VNet.

Never let address ranges overlap with other VNets or with your **on-premises** network (the one in your own offices and buildings): overlapping networks can't be connected later without renumbering everything.

A **network security group (NSG)** is a list of allow and deny rules for traffic, like a guest list, attached to a subnet or to one VM's network card (the virtual plug through which that VM sends and receives traffic). Each rule has a priority from 100 to 4096; Azure checks from the lowest number up, and the first rule that matches decides. NSGs remember connections: if a request is allowed in, its reply is allowed back out automatically.

Default rules allow traffic inside the VNet and Azure's own health checks (regular automatic tests that a resource is alive), and deny everything else coming in; traffic going out to the internet is allowed. Rules can use named groups of addresses, called **service tags** (`Internet`, `Storage.WestEurope`), instead of raw numbers. For VMs that must reach the internet, add a **NAT gateway**, which gives their outgoing traffic a fixed public address; Azure is retiring the older automatic outbound access.
concepts.code:
az network vnet create -g rg-net -n vnet-app --address-prefixes 10.10.0.0/16 \
  --subnet-name snet-web --subnet-prefixes 10.10.1.0/24

# Allow HTTPS (port 443) in from the internet
az network nsg create -g rg-net -n nsg-web
az network nsg rule create -g rg-net --nsg-name nsg-web -n allow-https \
  --priority 100 --direction Inbound --access Allow --protocol Tcp \
  --source-address-prefixes Internet --destination-port-ranges 443

# Attach the NSG to the subnet
az network vnet subnet update -g rg-net --vnet-name vnet-app -n snet-web \
  --network-security-group nsg-web

az network nsg rule list -g rg-net --nsg-name nsg-web --include-default -o table
takeaways: VNet = a private address range in one region, split into subnets
NSG rules: lowest priority number wins, and replies to allowed traffic are allowed automatically
Peering doesn't pass traffic along to a third VNet
Plan address ranges that don't overlap, up front
pitfalls: Picking overlapping address ranges, which makes later peering or connections to your office network impossible without renumbering.

quiz.q: An NSG has rule 200 Deny TCP 443 from Internet and rule 300 Allow TCP 443 from Internet. Is inbound HTTPS from the internet allowed?
options: Yes, the higher number takes precedence
No, rule 200 has the lower number and matches first
It depends on the default rules
quiz.explain: Rules are checked in priority order, lowest number first, and checking stops at the first match.

quiz.q: VNet A peers with B, and B peers with C. Can A reach C directly?
options: Only if all are in the same region
quiz.explain: You need a direct peering, or a hub VNet with a device that forwards traffic.

concepts.name: Storage accounts and redundancy
concepts.summary: One storage account holds files (blobs) and a few other kinds of data; choose its kind, speed and how many copies Azure keeps.
concepts.why: Storage accounts sit underneath many Azure services, and the redundancy choice decides which failures your data survives.
concepts.body:
A **storage account** is Azure's basic place to keep data. One account offers four services: Blob storage for files of any kind, Queue storage for small messages passed between programs, Files for shared network drives, and Table for simple records looked up by a key. The next lesson covers blobs; the others come later.

The account name must be unique across all of Azure, 3 to 24 lowercase letters and digits, because it becomes part of the account's endpoints: blobs, for example, are reached at `https://<name>.blob.core.windows.net`.

Choices made at creation:

- **Kind and performance**: `StorageV2` (general purpose, Standard performance) for almost everything; Premium kinds for workloads that need very fast responses.
- **Redundancy**, picked as the account's **SKU** (Azure's word for a product variant and its price):
  - **LRS**: three copies in one datacenter.
  - **ZRS**: three copies spread over the region's availability zones.
  - **GRS**: LRS plus a copy in the paired region; RA-GRS also lets you read that copy.
  - **GZRS** / RA-GZRS: ZRS plus the copy in the paired region.

The copy in the other region is updated a moment after each change, so a failover to it can lose the last few seconds of writes. The account's `lastSyncTime` shows how far behind it is.

Secure defaults to set: block anonymous public reading of blobs, require TLS 1.2, and turn off **shared key** access. Every account comes with two account keys, master passwords that give full control to whoever holds them; turning them off makes every request sign in through Entra ID instead.
concepts.code:
az storage account create -g rg-data -n stordersprod01 \
  --kind StorageV2 --sku Standard_ZRS --location westeurope \
  --min-tls-version TLS1_2 \
  --allow-blob-public-access false \
  --allow-shared-key-access false

az storage account show -g rg-data -n stordersprod01 \
  --query "{sku:sku.name, blob:primaryEndpoints.blob}"
# { "sku": "Standard_ZRS", "blob": "https://stordersprod01.blob.core.windows.net/" }
takeaways: One account = blob, queue, file and table endpoints under a globally unique name
LRS < ZRS < GRS/GZRS in resilience and price
The copy in the paired region trails slightly behind
Prefer Entra ID sign-in and turn off shared keys
pitfalls: Choosing LRS for data that must survive a zone outage.

quiz.q: Which SKU keeps data available if one availability zone fails, without a copy in another region?
quiz.explain: ZRS writes every change to three zones in the region at the same time.

concepts.name: Blob Storage: containers, tiers and SAS
concepts.summary: Store files as blobs in containers, pick hot, cool, cold or archive tiers, and hand out temporary access links safely.
concepts.why: Blob Storage is where Azure apps keep uploads, saved copies of data, website images and big piles of raw data.
concepts.body:
Blob Storage keeps files, which Azure calls **blobs**, each under a name like `2026/10/inv-1001.pdf`. Blobs are grouped into **blob containers** inside a storage account. This is a different meaning of "container" from Docker's: here it's just a named bucket of blobs, like a top-level folder. A blob's URL is `https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/<container>/<name>`.

There are no real folders: the `/` is just part of the name, and the portal shows it as folders. Turning on the **hierarchical namespace** (sold as Data Lake Storage) gives real folders that can be renamed in one step, which big data-analysis tools need. Most blobs are block blobs (ordinary files); append blobs suit logs that only grow, and page blobs hold VM disks.

**Access tiers** trade the price of storing against the price of reading:

- **Hot**: read often.
- **Cool**: read rarely; you pay for at least 30 days.
- **Cold**: read very rarely; at least 90 days.
- **Archive**: offline, at least 180 days. Before reading you must **rehydrate** the blob, copying it back online, which can take hours.

**Lifecycle management** rules move or delete blobs automatically by age, for example to Cool after 30 days and to Archive after 180.

To let someone upload or download a blob without giving them your login, create a **shared access signature (SAS)**: a URL with permissions and an expiry time built in, signed so nobody can alter them. Anyone holding the URL can use it until it expires, so keep the time short and the permissions minimal.

Prefer a **user delegation SAS**, signed with a key obtained through your Entra login rather than with an account key. It can be cancelled and traced to whoever made it; a SAS signed with an account key can only be cancelled by changing the key, which breaks everything else using it.

Protect data with **soft delete** (deleted blobs and containers can be restored for a set number of days), versioning (older copies are kept when a blob is overwritten), and immutability policies, which make data impossible to change or delete for a fixed period, as some laws require.
concepts.code:
az storage container create --account-name stordersprod01 -n invoices --auth-mode login

# Upload a file straight into the Cool tier, signed in with Entra ID
az storage blob upload --account-name stordersprod01 -c invoices \
  -n 2026/10/inv-1001.pdf -f ./inv-1001.pdf --tier Cool --auth-mode login

# A read-only user delegation SAS, valid for one hour
END=$(date -u -d "+1 hour" +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%MZ)
az storage blob generate-sas --account-name stordersprod01 -c invoices \
  -n 2026/10/inv-1001.pdf --permissions r --expiry "$END" \
  --auth-mode login --as-user --full-uri
# https://stordersprod01.blob.core.windows.net/invoices/2026/10/inv-1001.pdf?skoid=...&sig=...
takeaways: Container + blob name = one file; folders are just parts of the name
Hot, Cool, Cold, Archive: cheaper storage, but costlier and slower reading
Lifecycle rules change tiers and delete old blobs automatically
Prefer short-lived user delegation SAS links over ones signed with the account key
pitfalls: Putting blobs in Archive and expecting to read them immediately.
Handing out long-lived SAS links signed with the account key, which can only be cancelled by changing the key.

quiz.q: Why prefer a user delegation SAS over one signed with the account key?
options: It is signed through Entra ID, so it can be traced and cancelled without changing account keys
It is required for the Archive tier
quiz.explain: User delegation keys come from Entra ID and can be revoked on their own, without touching the account keys.

concepts.name: App Service web apps
concepts.summary: Host websites and web APIs without managing servers: plans, language versions, app settings and deployment slots.
concepts.why: App Service is the quickest production-ready way to run a web app without looking after servers yourself.
concepts.body:
A **web app** is a program people or other programs use over HTTP: a website, an online shop, or a **web API** that phone apps call. **Azure App Service** runs such programs for you. You hand it your code (Python, Node.js, .NET, Java, PHP) or a container image; Azure looks after the operating system and its updates, spreads traffic over copies of your app, and sets up HTTPS.

This kind of service, where you bring the code and Azure runs everything underneath, is called **platform as a service (PaaS)**.

Two resources are involved:

- The **App Service plan** is the computing power you pay for: Linux or Windows, a pricing tier (Free, Basic, Standard, Premium, Isolated) and how many **instances**, running copies of the underlying VM, it has. Several apps can share one plan.
- The web app itself: your site, with a default address `<name>.azurewebsites.net`.

Settings go into **app settings**, which your code reads as environment variables, so the same code runs with different settings in test and production. Scale **up** by moving the plan to a bigger tier, or **out** by adding instances, by hand or automatically with **autoscale** rules that react to load.

**Deployment slots** (Standard tier and up) are extra live copies of the app, such as `staging`, each with its own address. Deploy the new version to the slot, check it and let it warm up, then **swap** it with production: users move to the new version with no downtime. If something's wrong, swap back. Mark settings that belong to one environment, like the production database address, as slot settings so they stay put during a swap.

Also worth knowing: built-in sign-in for your users ("Easy Auth"), your own domain names with free certificates, and **Always On**, which keeps the app loaded so the first visitor after a quiet period doesn't wait while it starts up from scratch (a **cold start**).
concepts.code:
# From a folder containing a Python web app (Flask, FastAPI or Django):
az webapp up --name orders-web-dev --resource-group rg-web \
  --runtime "PYTHON:3.12" --sku B1

# These become environment variables inside the app
az webapp config appsettings set -g rg-web -n orders-web-dev \
  --settings FEATURE_X=on LOG_LEVEL=info

# Release with no downtime using a slot (needs Standard or higher)
az appservice plan update -g rg-web -n <plan-name> --sku S1
az webapp deployment slot create -g rg-web -n orders-web-dev --slot staging
az webapp deployment slot swap -g rg-web -n orders-web-dev --slot staging --target-slot production
takeaways: Plan = computing power you pay for; app = the site running on it
App settings become environment variables
Slots + swap give releases with no downtime and instant rollback
Scale up = bigger tier; scale out = more instances
pitfalls: Putting a heavy background job in the same plan as the production site, so both fight over the same instances.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of deploying to a staging slot and swapping?
options: The new version is warmed up before receiving traffic, and rollback is just a swap back
It moves the app to another region
quiz.explain: The swap sends traffic to copies that are already running, so users see no downtime.

concepts.name: Pricing, budgets and cost analysis
concepts.summary: How Azure bills you, how to estimate costs, and how to watch spending with cost analysis and budgets.
concepts.why: Cloud bills grow quietly; knowing how each service is charged and setting budgets early avoids nasty surprises.
concepts.body:
Azure charges each thing you use separately, by a **meter**: VM time per second, stored data per gigabyte per month plus a tiny fee per read or write, data sent out of Azure per gigabyte, function runs per million, and so on. The same service can cost very differently by region, tier and redundancy.

Tools to know:

- The **pricing calculator** estimates a design before you build it.
- **Cost analysis** (in Cost Management): actual and forecast cost, grouped by subscription, resource group, service or tag.
- **Budgets**: an amount per month, quarter or year on a subscription or resource group, with alert levels (say 80% spent, or 100% forecast) that email people.
- **Azure Advisor**: recommendations, such as idle or oversized resources.

A budget alert can also start an automatic response through an **action group**, a saved list of whom to notify and what to run. But a budget **never stops** spending by itself.

Habits that keep costs predictable:

- Tag resources with owner, environment and cost center, so the bill can be split.
- Delete dev resource groups when done; deallocate idle VMs; schedule auto-shutdown for dev VMs.
- Watch the classic surprises: data sent out of Azure to the internet (**egress**), premium disks left behind after deleting a VM, the volume of stored logs, public IP addresses, and network devices that charge by the hour even when idle.

Prices change, so always check the region's pricing page rather than numbers you remember.
concepts.code:
# A monthly budget of 500 on one resource group
az consumption budget create --budget-name dev-monthly \
  --amount 500 --category cost --time-grain monthly \
  --start-date 2026-11-01 --end-date 2027-10-31 \
  --resource-group rg-orders-dev

# Cost so far this month per resource group, asked straight from the Cost Management API
az rest --method post \
  --url "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/providers/Microsoft.CostManagement/query?api-version=2023-11-01" \
  --body '{"type":"ActualCost","timeframe":"MonthToDate",
    "dataset":{"granularity":"None","aggregation":{"cost":{"name":"Cost","function":"Sum"}},
    "grouping":[{"type":"Dimension","name":"ResourceGroupName"}]}}'
takeaways: Every service bills per meter; region and tier change the price
Budgets alert but never stop resources
Tags let you split the bill by team and project
Egress, logs, leftover disks and idle network devices are common surprises
pitfalls: Expecting a budget to cap spending: it only sends alerts or runs actions you set up.

quiz.q: Your budget of 500 hits 100%. What does Azure do by default?
options: Sends the configured alerts; resources keep running
quiz.explain: Budgets only notify; stopping anything needs your own automation.

concepts.name: Managed identities and DefaultAzureCredential
concepts.summary: Give code running in Azure its own Entra identity, with no passwords or keys to store, replace or leak.
concepts.why: Managed identities take passwords and keys out of your settings, which is where most leaked cloud credentials come from.
concepts.body:
Programs that call other services need **credentials**: something that proves who they are, such as a password, a key, or a connection string with a password inside. Kept in settings files or code, credentials get copied, forgotten and leaked.

A **managed identity** removes the problem. It is a service principal whose secret Azure creates, stores and replaces itself. Code running on the resource asks a special address that exists only inside Azure for an access token, and never sees a secret at all. On VMs that address is the **Instance Metadata Service** (`169.254.169.254`); App Service, Functions and Container Apps offer an equivalent.

Two kinds:

- **System-assigned**: created with one resource and deleted with it. Simple: one identity per resource.
- **User-assigned**: a resource of its own (`Microsoft.ManagedIdentity/userAssignedIdentities`) that you attach to any number of resources. It survives when the app is deleted and recreated, can be given roles *before* the app exists, and can trust outside systems (the workload identity federation lesson). Prefer it in production and when resources are created from code files (**infrastructure as code**, the Bicep lesson).

The workflow: switch on the identity, give it a role on the target (Key Vault Secrets User, Storage Blob Data Contributor, a database user), then call the target with Azure's **SDK**: the ready-made code Microsoft publishes for using Azure from Python, .NET, Java, JavaScript and Go.

In code, use **`DefaultAzureCredential`** from the `azure-identity` package (the example is Python; the other languages have the same thing). It tries a list of sign-in sources in order: environment variables, workload identity, managed identity, then developer logins such as the Azure CLI. So the same code runs on your laptop (as you) and in Azure (as the identity).

If several user-assigned identities are attached, set `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` so the right one is picked. In production you can use `ManagedIdentityCredential` directly, which starts faster and never falls back to something unexpected.
concepts.code:
# pip install azure-identity azure-storage-blob
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.storage.blob import BlobServiceClient

# On your laptop: uses your `az login`. In Azure: uses the managed identity.
cred = DefaultAzureCredential()
svc = BlobServiceClient("https://stordersprod01.blob.core.windows.net", credential=cred)

for blob in svc.get_container_client("invoices").list_blobs(name_starts_with="2026/10/"):
    print(blob.name)   # 2026/10/inv-1001.pdf

# Setup (bash):
# az webapp identity assign -g rg-web -n orders-web
# az role assignment create --assignee <principalId> \
#   --role "Storage Blob Data Reader" --scope <storage account id>
takeaways: Managed identity = credentials Azure manages; no secrets in settings or code
System-assigned lives and dies with its resource; user-assigned is reusable
It still needs a role assignment on the target
DefaultAzureCredential runs unchanged on your laptop and in Azure
pitfalls: Switching on the identity but forgetting the role assignment, then getting 403 errors.

quiz.q: Why choose a user-assigned identity for an app deployed from Bicep files?
options: It is the only kind that works with Key Vault
It can be created and given roles before the app, and survives the app being recreated
It works outside Azure without credentials
quiz.explain: A user-assigned identity has its own lifecycle, so its roles are ready before the app starts and don't vanish with it.

quiz.q: On a developer laptop, which credential does DefaultAzureCredential usually end up using?
options: The developer's Azure CLI or code-editor login
quiz.explain: There is no managed identity address on a laptop, so the list falls through to developer logins.

concepts.name: Key Vault: secrets, keys and certificates
concepts.summary: Keep secrets, encryption keys and certificates in one guarded place, read through Azure roles and managed identities.
concepts.why: Secrets that can't be eliminated belong in Key Vault, not in code, deployment scripts or plain app settings.
concepts.body:
**Azure Key Vault** stores three kinds of item:

- **Secrets**: any sensitive string, such as a database password or an **API key** (the password a program uses for another company's service).
- **Keys**: encryption keys for scrambling and signing data. The work happens inside the vault, on tamper-proof hardware called an **HSM** (hardware security module) in the Premium tier or Managed HSM, so the key itself never leaves.
- **Certificates**: HTTPS certificates, which Key Vault can renew automatically with supported issuers.

Every item keeps its old versions. An address without a version, like `https://kv-orders.vault.azure.net/secrets/db-password`, returns the latest one.

Decide who may read what with the Azure RBAC permission model (the default for new vaults) rather than the older access policies. Typical roles: **Key Vault Secrets User** (read secret values), **Key Vault Secrets Officer** (manage secrets), **Key Vault Crypto User**, **Key Vault Administrator**. Give the app's managed identity Secrets User on just that one vault.

Soft delete is always on (7 to 90 days), so a deleted vault or secret can be restored, and its name stays taken until it is permanently removed (purged). Turn on **purge protection** in production so nobody can permanently destroy keys before that period ends.

App Service, Functions and Container Apps can read secrets without code changes. An app setting whose value is `@Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=...)` is a **Key Vault reference**: the platform fetches the secret using the app's identity and hands it to your code as a normal environment variable. Close the vault to the internet with a private endpoint (an Advanced lesson) and public access turned off.
concepts.code:
az keyvault create -g rg-sec -n kv-orders-prod --enable-purge-protection true
az keyvault secret set --vault-name kv-orders-prod -n db-password --value 'S3cr3t!'

# Let the web app's identity read secrets in this vault only
KV_ID=$(az keyvault show -n kv-orders-prod --query id -o tsv)
az role assignment create --assignee "$APP_PRINCIPAL_ID" \
  --role "Key Vault Secrets User" --scope "$KV_ID"

# Key Vault reference: the app sees the secret as environment variable DB_PASSWORD
az webapp config appsettings set -g rg-web -n orders-web --settings \
  "DB_PASSWORD=@Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=https://kv-orders-prod.vault.azure.net/secrets/db-password/)"
takeaways: Secrets, keys and certificates, all with version history
Use the RBAC model; give the app's identity Secrets User on one vault
Soft delete is always on; add purge protection in production
Key Vault references put secrets into app settings without code
pitfalls: Recreating a deleted vault with the same name and getting a conflict: it is still soft-deleted until purged or recovered.

quiz.q: Which role should an app identity that only reads secret values get?
quiz.explain: Secrets User lets it read secret values and nothing more.

quiz.q: What does purge protection add on top of soft delete?
options: A guarantee that deleted items cannot be permanently removed before the retention period ends
quiz.explain: Without it, an admin could soft-delete and then immediately purge.

concepts.name: Infrastructure as code with Bicep
concepts.summary: Describe resources in Bicep files with parameters, outputs and modules, and deploy them the same way every time.
concepts.why: Infrastructure as code makes environments repeatable and reviewable; Bicep is Azure's own language for it.
concepts.body:
Clicking resources together in the portal works once, but it's hard to repeat exactly for test and production. Infrastructure as code means describing your resources in text files instead, so they can be reviewed, kept in version history and deployed again identically. **Bicep** is Azure's own language for this.

Bicep is declarative, like SQL: you describe what should exist, and ARM works out what to create or change. Before sending, the `az` command converts (**compiles**) your Bicep file into an ARM **template**, the JSON format ARM understands. Nothing else keeps a record of what you deployed: Azure itself is the record.

Building blocks:

- `param`: an input value, or **parameter**, with a type, a default, and checks such as `@allowed`, `@minLength` or `@secure()` (keep the value out of logs).
- `var`: a value computed inside the file.
- `resource sa 'Provider/type@apiVersion' = { ... }`: a resource with a **symbolic name** (`sa`) you use elsewhere, as in `sa.id`. Using it also tells Bicep to create that resource first.
- `output`: values handed back after the deployment.
- `module`: another Bicep file used as a building block, the unit of reuse. **Azure Verified Modules** are well-tested ones Microsoft publishes (`br/public:avm/...`).
- `existing`: points at a resource that is already deployed, without managing it.

Functions such as `resourceGroup().location` and `uniqueString(resourceGroup().id)` keep a file reusable. The second turns its input into short random-looking text, always the same for the same input, so names are unique per resource group yet stable between deployments.

Deploy with `az deployment group create` (or `sub`, `mg`, `tenant` to deploy at those levels), keeping one `.bicepparam` parameter file per environment. Run **what-if** before production to preview what will be created, changed and deleted. The Bicep extension for VS Code completes and checks every resource type as you type.
takeaways: Bicep compiles to an ARM template; Azure itself is the record of what exists
Using a symbolic name makes Bicep create that resource first
Modules are the unit of reuse; check Azure Verified Modules first
Run what-if before production deployments
